[01:14:57] is you want small models that are capable.
[01:14:59] You do not want big, bloated models that cost a lot to serve,
[01:15:03] even if that minimizes training cost.
[01:15:05] And so what you really want is something that you would call
[01:15:09] as "overtrained."
[01:15:10] I put that in quotes because, really, overtraining
[01:15:12] is what we want.
[01:15:13] That's the right amount of training.
[01:15:14] And if you look at all the models that were released
[01:15:17] in the early days, like GPT-3--
[01:15:19] this was under-trained for sure, three tokens per parameter.
[01:15:22] Chinchilla gets to the modern ratio of 20 per parameter.
[01:15:25] And then for a while, people were at 20 per parameter.
[01:15:27] And this is the era, I think, where
[01:15:29] there wasn't that much serving of these models.
[01:15:31] The models were cool, but it wasn't being served at scale.
[01:15:34] And then as you start to move to eras where serving becomes very
[01:15:38] real, now you're overtraining these models,
[01:15:40] and now you've moved into MoEs, and you're
[01:15:41] making all these trade-offs to optimize inference serving.
[01:15:44] So I think Chinchilla is important,
[01:15:47] not because I think the 20-to-1 ratio is the one golden ratio.
[01:15:51] If you're doing stuff for research, it might be.
[01:15:54] But I think the reason why it's important
[01:15:56] is because it tells us quite a bit about how
[01:15:58] we should be fitting scaling laws
[01:16:00] and how to think about scaling laws.
[01:16:02] OK, one final thing I'll end with Chinchilla-wise
[01:16:06] and otherwise for scaling is IsoFLOP
[01:16:08] have been one of the things that, I think,
[01:16:10] has a research tool have endured.
[01:16:12] IsoFLOP are very easy to execute.
[01:16:14] You fix a FLOPS budget, and then you
[01:16:16] sweep over all of the other degrees of freedom
[01:16:18] to see what the surface looks like.
[01:16:20] And this gives you, in general, fairly reliable readings
[01:16:25] of how different parameters vary as a function
[01:16:28] of your free parameters.
[01:16:31] People have done this for-- or actually, one of my students
[01:16:34] did this for diffusion models.
[01:16:36] The MoE study I talked about was a IsoFLOP-style design.
[01:16:40] If you're ever in a situation where you're thinking,
[01:16:42] how am I going to decide all these trade-offs,
[01:16:45] IsoFLOP is always a good default.
[01:16:48] OK, so to wrap up everything for today,
[01:16:53] there's this idea that we have this log-linear regularity
[01:16:56] between the amount of resources we put in
[01:16:59] and the performance we get out.
[01:17:00] And it extends to a wide variety of things, model parameters,
[01:17:03] compute, sparsity level of your MoE.
[01:17:06] And that lets you do a lot of the things
[01:17:08] that I was talking about earlier, as arbitrary choices,
[01:17:11] but do it in a much more evidence-driven way, hopefully.
[01:17:14] And so this allows us to have engineering at scale
[01:17:18] without explicitly relying on doing big model training runs.
[01:17:22] And hopefully, you remember, I think all
[01:17:25] the different components here.
[01:17:26] Data scaling is this very natural object,
[01:17:28] just the exponent is a little bit strange.
[01:17:30] Model scaling allows you to do all these cool engineering
[01:17:32] things.
[01:17:33] And then finally, scaling is this very cool,
[01:17:36] robust predictor, let's call it, for how
[01:17:38] to try to do engineering at a large scale.
